replying_to: Replying to Ripple Attention for Visual Perception with Sub-quadratic Complexity
display_title: Official Review of Paper2730 by Reviewer Siyf

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work focuses on the problem of strengthening the inductive bias of Transformer-based models within the computer vision domain. This problem is of interest in the field, as the increased flexibility of Transformers comes with a high price tag in terms of training data requirements.

To this end, the authors propose to inject a learned 2D spatial locality prior, called Ripple, into the Transformer's attention blocks. Concretely, the contribution of each key token to the response is scaled by a learned scalar weight, which is shared by all key tokens found at the same chessboard distance from the query. A soft prior is placed onto the learned weights, favoring higher magnitude weights for small chessboard distances, and thus encouraging 2D spatial locality.

Although the method is general, being applicable to any kernelized version of attention, the authors focus on its application only in the context of linearized softmax kernel approximations, due to certain desirable computational properties. For such linear models, they show that dynamic programming can be used to efficiently forward propagate attention, keeping the sub-quadratic complexity of the vanilla (unweighted) linear variant.

Experiments on image classification and object detection tasks show that Ripple, when applied to linearized models, can recover and even exceed the accuracy of the original softmax-based attention model. From the point of view of empirical inference speed, results are mixed, with significant speedups being observed in one classification experiment, but no speedups being noted for object detection.
content.main_review:
### Strengths:

- *Problem importance*: this work lies at the confluence of two hot topics in the field right now, namely the need for stronger inductive bias in Transformers and the need to improve their scalability.
- *Presentation style*: the paper is clearly written, well structured and easy to follow.
- *Novelty*: while not being the first time locality priors are proposed, up to my knowledge, the proposed method is sufficiently different from previous approaches, especially given its computational friendliness compared to alternatives.

### Weaknesses:

- *Strong complexity claims*: I am not convinced that the method is truly linear in the number of tokens, at least not for the typical use-case in computer vision, in which tokens become denser in image space.

  The authors claim in section 3.3 "[..] given a reasonable hyper-parameter choice of \tau, the algorithm can achieve linear observed time in sequence length". However, note that commonly, in computer vision, one scales the input not by increasing the field of view of the camera, but rather by increasing the resolution of the image or of the token sampling grid. Hence, the receptive field radius, when measured in tokens, must also scale linearly with the resolution, in order to capture objects and context at the same scale in the physical world. Hence, one would expect that $R$, $R_{max}$ and $\hat{r}$ would need to increase linearly with the image resolution in order to keep the accuracy of the computer vision task. This implies a $O(T^{\frac{3}{2}})$ complexity, which is still sub-quadratic, but not linear. I note that the authors themselves mention this in Appendix B, Table 5, which seems to contradict the linear complexity claim in section 3.3.

- *Experimental procedure - relevance of running time vs. resolution experiment*: In light of the observation above, I consider that the analysis in Figure 2 is not entirely relevant for the typical computer vision use-case in which resolution (as opposed to camera field of view) is increasing. From what I understand, while varying the number of tokens, $R_{max}$ was kept constant in Figure 2, instead of scaling linearly with the input resolution.

- *Experimental results - reduced impact for detection tasks*: Except for small objects, the proposed method does not seem to improve detection precision (Table 3), nor does it provide any inference time speedup.

- *Experimental scope - accuracy analysis in the quadratic case:* The paper proposes two contributions, i.e. a generally applicable locality prior and efficient inference for the particular case of linear kernels. However, the accuracy impact of the former is only evaluated in case of linear kernels.

  Granted, the Ripple prior is attractive in the linear setting, but it is still a generally applicable inductive bias that can potentially improve accuracy of the state-of-the-art softmax kernels. Adding a comparison against other inductive biases (e.g. CONVIT) in the quadratic complexity setting would help understand the suitability of the proposed bias from a machine learning perspective, and also clarify the performance gap introduced by the linear approximations for the proposed method.

- *Analysis of core design choice - the ripple weights parametrization scheme:* the method requires the prediction of $R$ scalars ($\alpha_r$) at each query point using a neural network. It is not clear whether this parametrization is really needed.

  While the authors do experiment with exponentially decayed spatial weights, these values are not learned and may be a poor match to the weights learned by the stick-breaking transformation. It would be interesting to see a curve of the weights overlaid over the fixed exponential weights. Such an analysis may not only reveal the discrepancy, but also shed light on whether:

  (1) There are simpler parametric curves that could be used, further increasing the speed of the method.
  (2) It could be possible to use a logarithmic scale for the ripples and still match the curves well. That is, ripple thickness would grow exponentially (base 2) when moving away from the query token (currently all ripples have thickness of exactly 1 token). If a curve match is revealed, such a method would lower the complexity to $O(T log T)$, because the SAT trick could still be used to propagate ripples of any thickness.

### Minor comments:

- In Algorithm 1, Output field: $W(i,j,t)$ and $W(i,j,t-1)$ should read $W(i,j,r)$ and $W(i,j,r-1)$
- In Equation 1, Attn($q_n$, K, V) is a row vector according to the scalar softmax formula, but is a column vector according to the matrix formula (right hand side):

   - $V^{\top}$ has size $C \times M$
   - $\text{softmax}(K q_n)$ has size $M \times 1$
   - $V^{\top} \text{softmax}(K q_n)$ has size $C \times1$

   For mathematical correctness, one could re-write the matrix form as $\text{softmax}(K q_n)^{\top} V$, which would result in a row vector as well for the RHS as well.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, I think the paper addresses a relevant problem. The proposed solution, while not the first locality prior proposed for attention in Transformers, is elegant and computationally appealing. This paper is clearly written and well structured, and I enjoyed reading it. 

However, my *main concern* is the assumption that the locality prior strength, for the method as proposed, is independent on the number of tokens. This makes, in my view, some of the complexity claims too strong, and the speed measurement experiments less relevant for the typical practical use-case (in which scalability with input resolution, as opposed to field of view, is relevant).

My *secondary concern* is that for object detection the method does not show a clear benefit, although for image classification the method shows convincing results.

Finally, while many open points are carefully considered, my *minor concerns* are related to two loose ends in the analysis, as I perceive them:

- How does the locality prior look like in practice? Is the ripple parameterization scheme with $O(R)$=$O(T^{1/2})$ parameters really necessary, or would a logarithmic scheme with thicker ripples suffice, e.g. one having only $O(\log R)$=$O(\log T)$ parameters? 
- Complexity aside, how does the proposed inductive bias stack up against other state-of-the-art (i.e. un-approximated) approaches? 

Given all of the above, I think in the current form, this work is marginally below acceptance threshold. However, my suggestion to the authors is to relax the complexity claims and re-run the empirical running time analysis assuming the $R_{\text{max}}$ increased linearly with $\sqrt{T}$. If a clear speedup is still observed in this scenario, this could make an argument for an increased impact for this work for publication. 

Apart from this, including an analysis of the locality weight curves and possible logarithmic parameterization schemes would be a welcome addition. This may even reveal that further complexity/empirical speed improvements are possible, strengthening experimental results and complexity guarantees.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2730 by Reviewer Siyf

content.title: Response to Reviewer Siyf (1/2)
content.comment:
Thanks a lot for your insightful comments and kind suggestions! Here are our responses:
> Q1: On *Strong complexity claims* & *Experimental procedure - relevance of running time vs. resolution experiment*: ...Hence, one would expect that $R$, $R_{max}$ and $\tau$ would need to increase linearly with the image resolution in order to keep the accuracy of the computer vision task. ...contradict the linear complexity claim in section 3.3.

A1: Thanks for raising this point! In the case where the resolution increases linearly, one could in principle increase the size of vicinal groups (i.e., the ripple thickness) correspondingly to keep the same accuracy, with $R_{max}$ left as constant. One may also use a larger number of thinner vicinal groups (increasing $R_{max}$) to process finer-grained details for further performance gain; in general, our model is a flexible framework that allows such trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. As for the complexity, we set $R_{max}$ to a constant value (equivalent to restricting $\tau$) throughout experiments and find it works well; therefore we think it is reasonable to state that our model can achieve the linear time complexity.
 
> Q2: *Experimental results - reduced impact for detection tasks*: Except for small objects, the proposed method does not seem to improve detection precision (Table 3), nor does it provide any inference time speedup.

A2: The performance of ripple attention for detection tasks is bottlenecked by the adopted linearized attention mechanism; our model gives a clear performance boost over vanilla linearized attention. In addition, it is known that vanilla detection transformers perform poorly at detecting small objects [1, 2]. Although not outperforming regular softmax attention, ripple attention does better in smaller scales, verifying the effectiveness of the introduced locality bias.

Reference:

[1] Carion, N., Massa, F., Synnaeve, G., Usunier, N., Kirillov, A., & Zagoruyko, S. (2020, August). End-to-end object detection with transformers. In European Conference on Computer Vision (pp. 213-229). Springer, Cham.

[2] Gao, P., Zheng, M., Wang, X., Dai, J., & Li, H. (2021). Fast convergence of detr with spatially modulated co-attention. arXiv:2101.07448.
 
> Q3: *Experimental scope - accuracy analysis in the quadratic case*: ...but it is still a generally applicable inductive bias that can potentially improve accuracy of the state-of-the-art softmax kernels. Adding a comparison against other inductive biases (e.g. CONVIT) in the quadratic complexity setting...

A3: The linearized attention mechanism is essential for ripple attention, as it (1) decomposes the computation among queries and keys, and (2) computes the key-value statistics via summation (see equation 2), which allows us to do partial reductions over defined vicinal groups. Although generally applicable by intuition, such rippling effect is ambiguous in the case of regular softmax attention, as it does not have a clear notion of partial reduction over vicinal groups. We refer the reviewer to Appendix A for more detailed discussion. For reference, we implement a ripple version of softmax attention by simply adding the rippling effect to the attention weights as a relative positional bias. The result on ImageNet dataset is 69.9% in top-1 accuracy, which is much lower than the regular softmax attention (72.2%) and ripple attention (73.0%). Although this may not be the best approach to implementing the rippling effect in the softmax-attention sense, this result implies the necessity of adopting linearized attention. Investigating how to decouple the locality bias and linearized attention mechanism would be an interesting future work.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Siyf (2/2)
content.comment:
> Q4: *Analysis of core design choice - the ripple weights parametrization scheme*: ...It would be interesting to see a curve of the weights overlaid over the fixed exponential weights. Such an analysis may not only reveal the discrepancy, but also shed light on whether: (1) There are simpler parametric curves that could be used, further increasing the speed of the method. (2) It could be possible to use a logarithmic scale for the ripples and still match the curves well. That is, ripple thickness would grow exponentially (base 2) when moving away from the query token (currently all ripples have thickness of exactly 1 token). If a curve match is revealed, such a method would lower the complexity to $\mathcal{O}(T\log T)$, because the SAT trick could still be used to propagate ripples of any thickness.

A4: Thanks for your insightful comments! We add the experiment that investigates the performance of a curve with fewer parameters (the ripples are getting exponentially thicker, e.g. 1, 2, 4, 8, …, which we denoted by logarithmic ripple). With the same hyper-parameter setting (including the seed), we observe logarithmic ripple performs worse than the dense one (73.26 vs. 74.43, as shown in Table 8, Appendix D.2). However, in terms of empirical running analysis (see Figure 3 in Appendix D.2), we found logarithmic ripple runs as fast as base ripple (with a constant $R_{max}$) and becomes much more efficient than the dense one (with $R_{max}$ increased linearly) as the number of tokens increases. Also note that even the dense version runs much faster than the softmax attention and the naïve implementation. This justifies that our model defines a flexible framework and allows one to trade-off between accuracy and efficiency in various ways.

Besides, we also plot the evolution (Figure 4 in Appendix D.3) of Jensen-Shannon divergence between distributions induced by stick-breaking transforms and fixed exponential weights. It indicates that our parameterization scheme can learn to balance global and local information and tend to favor local correlations. However, plateauing at a large JSD value indicates that ripple attention remains to be significantly different from the fixed weights and is able to capture complex long-range dependencies.
 
> Q5: Complexity aside, how does the proposed inductive bias stack up against other state-of-the-art (i.e. un-approximated) approaches?

A5: For un-approximated models, we compare ripple attention to ConViT, a performant baseline that initializes the attention weights as a convolutional kernel. The fact that ripple attention performs competitively with ConViT demonstrates its effectiveness. For other work that modifies the transformer architecture such as introducing convolutional modules, our work is orthogonal to them, and it is interesting to investigate how they can be combined to improve the overall vision transformer model.

content.title: Feedback to authors
content.comment:
I thank the authors for their detailed answers and also for spending time and effort to perform additional experiments.

Regarding my main concern (complexity claims): I agree with the authors that using thicker vicinal groups is a theoretical approach that could reach the linear complexity claims with respect to resolution increase. Of course, experiments in which input resolution is varied would need to be carried out to validate this claim empirically: to gauge the exact speedups (i.e. the empirical running time/memory consumption curves in Figure 2 may look different under this setup) together with the accuracy for each resolution. To my understanding, one would need to keep the thickness of the ripples spatially constant in this experiment, to generalize the current approach to varying resolutions (this is somewhat different than the logarithmic ripple thickness case the authors also explore in Figure 3).

Regarding my minor concern (impact for detection tasks): I agree that transformers are performing worse at detecting smaller scale objects, and hence the bias itself is helpful in this particular case (if one is restricted to using transformer-based models of course). However, the method is still slower than the nonlinear version (inference time 0.065s vs 0.0059s) while also less accurate overall (40.5% AP vs 41.0% AP) - Table 3. This limits the practical impact of the proposed method for detection tasks.

Regarding A3-A5 (improvements/analyses): I thank the authors for the additional experiments, which I think provide more insight into the tradeoffs and alternatives.

After reading the other reviews, and since I consider that my major/minor concerns are still not addressed in the revised form, I keep my recommendation.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents ripple attention, which assigns different attention weights to patches at different distances. Ripple attention provides a feasible way of utilizing the locality bias in natural images, while still preserving the long-range modeling capability of the attention mechanism. The spatial weights are derived by a stick-breaking transformation and a dynamic programming algorithm is designed to execute the proposed ripple attention in linear observed time. Experiments show that the proposed ripple attention achieves some performance gain over baseline methods in image classification and object detection tasks.
content.main_review:
It is widely acknowledged that locality bias in images (patches have stronger correlations with spatially closer patches) is very important and should not be neglected in vision transformers. The proposed ripple attention is a technically sound and neat solution to address this issue. However, the concerns come from the following aspects. 

First, there are many other ways to utilize locality bias in vision transformers, such as more complex positional embedding, local attention windows, or combination with convolutions. Ripple attention, although it is very neat, does not appear to be the most promising solution. In the experiments section, ripple attention is not compared with other methods that try to inject locality bias into transformer design (e.g. some work cited in the related work section).

Second, ripple attention is built upon linearized attention mechanism. It could be looked on as its advantage in complexity, but I would rather think of it as its disadvantage in performance. This reviewer appreciates the ablation study which compares ripple attention with fixed exponentially decayed weights. The advantage of ripple attention demonstrates the necessary of stick-breaking transformation. However, this reviewer does not understand the efforts put to the complexity reduction from O(HWR^2) to O(HWR), as R_{max} is set to 4 in the final implementation. 

Overall, this reviewer is not convinced that ripple attention strikes a good tradeoff between complexity and performance, although it provides a neat solution to leverage locality bias in vision transformers.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method is technically sound and addresses an important problem. The paper is well-written and easy to follow. However, the authors do not provide enough evidence that the proposed method is the best solution to address the problem of interest. The experimental results are mostly conducted with baseline solutions not competing solutions.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2730 by Reviewer wmN7

content.title: Response to Reviewer wmN7
content.comment:
Thanks a lot for your feedback and thoughtful comments! Here are our responses:
> Q1: …Ripple attention, although it is very neat, does not appear to be the most promising solution. In the experiments section, ripple attention is not compared with other methods that try to inject locality bias into transformer design (e.g. some work cited in the related work section)… the authors do not provide enough evidence that the proposed method is the best solution to address the problem of interest.

A1: Thanks for raising this point! We add a paragraph in Section 6 to discuss this point. To summarize, our method is different from previous methods in that we directly model the locality inside the attention mechanism while still preserving the ability to capture global dependencies, without introducing convolutional kernels or limiting receptive fields. Furthermore, ripple attention runs in sub-quadratic complexity so that the runtime/space bottleneck in vision transformers can be largely alleviated. This implies that one could potentially incorporate the relative locality into the attention mechanism while enjoying the same complexity as convolutional modules, which we think is a solid contribution to  the community. In this setting, direct comparison to vanilla linearized or regular attention should suffice to demonstrate the effectiveness of our work. For reference, we also compare it against ConViT, a performant baseline that directly improves on the softmax attention by initializing attention maps as a convolutional kernel. Our model performs comparably to ConViT with an asymptotically faster runtime, verifying the effectiveness of ripple attention. Finally, our work is orthogonal to previous work that modifies the transformer architecture and it is worth exploring their combination to improve the overall transformer network.
 
> Q2: …However, this reviewer does not understand the efforts put to the complexity reduction from $\mathcal{O}(HWR^2)$ to $\mathcal{O}(HWR)$, as $R_{max}$ is set to 4 in the final implementation.

A2: In terms of the complexity, the naïve implementation not only runs with quadratic complexity in sequence length, but also suffers from a large constant, which is at least 8 times larger than that of our DP version (Please see Appendix A for more details). Therefore, even though we set $R_{max}$ to 4 in practice to avoid unnecessary computations, the naïve implementation runs with much more expensive computational costs. This is also reflected in the empirical running comparison (Figure 2).

display_title: Official Review of Paper2730 by Reviewer MU1H

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors start from the hypothesis that current vision transformer lacks the ability to extract local information in images, thus some locality constraint is needed to improve the performance. The proposed algorithm contains a spatial weighting scheme which is designed to put higher weights on local patches and lower weights on remote patches. A stick-breaking transform is used for deciding the spatial weights. And also a dynamic programming method is adopted for computational efficiency. The authors test their algorithm on image classification and detection tasks and also conduct some ablation study to analyze the design of the algorithm.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

+   The algorithm is clearly introduced. The usage stick-breaking transform and dynamic programming is delicate.
+   The efficient algorithm for backprop is interesting.
+   The ablation study in Table 4 is well-designed.


Weaknesses / Other comments:

-    This paper is motivated by the conjecture that current vision transformer lacks the ability to extract local statistics in images and therefore is not the best design for vision tasks. But I think the authors haven't provide enough evidence to support their motivation. First of all, is ViT really not able to extract local information? In fact, some work has shown that ViT can also learn local attention despite it's computed globally [1]. Another question is, do we really more locality constraint in ViT? On one hand, locality constraint may have its own drawbacks, eg., making the model less robustness under image corruptions [2]. On the other hand, even for regular tasks of classification and detection on clean images, the authors did not show a very promising results of their model with locality bias. RIPPLE is not as good as CONVIT, another model with locality bias, on classification tasks, and also does not show advantages on the detection task.
-    Discussion on some other baselines is missed. A bunch of works have also introduce locality bias into transformers, eg., constraining the range of attention [3], or combining convolution and self-attention [4]. Experiments with all these baselines can be time-consuming, but at least some justification of the relation between RIPPLE and the prior arts is helpful.
-    The authors may also compare to some baselines of linearized attention. It seems the authors make some changes on previous linearized attention schemes, such as using a two-layer MLP instead of random features. Some ablation study on these changes can help clarify the contribution of the locality constraint itself.
-    In the experiments the authors show that a hard-coded spatial weights is worse than learning the weights using stick-breaking transformation (RIPPLE vs. Fixed-RIPPLE). So if we don't have any constraint on the spatial weighting (except for positivity and unit sum),  can the network still learn the local bias?
-    It seems the authors empirically choose the first 9 self-attention blocks to replace with RIPPLE. Does this setting apply to different tasks?



[1] Raghu M, Unterthiner T, Kornblith S, et al. Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2108.08810, 2021.

[2] Mao X, Qi G, Chen Y, et al. Towards Robust Vision Transformer[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2105.07926, 2021.

[3] Liu Z, Lin Y, Cao Y, et al. Swin transformer: Hierarchical vision transformer using shifted windows[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2103.14030, 2021.

[4] Srinivas A, Lin T Y, Parmar N, et al. Bottleneck transformers for visual recognition[C]//Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2021: 16519-16529.
content.summary_of_the_review: The algorithm is properly designed and sensitive. But the motivation is not convincing enough and the experimental results do not well support the statements from the authors.

content.title: Response to Reviewer MU1H
content.comment:
Thanks a lot for your review and thoughtful comments! Here are our responses:
> Q1: …First of all, is ViT really not able to extract local information? In fact, some work has shown that ViT can also learn local attention despite it's computed globally.

A1: Thanks for listing these insightful references! Now that ViT needs to implicitly learn to identify the locality (to some extent), it would be much more efficient for us to explicitly guide ViT to do so. In this case, the model would directly learn to balance global and local information, which is more effective and efficient than first trying to identify the locality without guidance and then learn to balance. Our experiments on CIFAR100 dataset clearly demonstrates this advantage, where the vanilla ViT fails to do well due to limited data while ripple attention outperforms ViT by a large margin.
 
> Q2: Another question is, do we really more locality constraint in ViT? On one hand, locality constraint may have its own drawbacks, eg., making the model less robustness under image corruptions [2]. On the other hand, even for regular tasks of classification and detection on clean images, the authors did not show a very promising results of their model with locality bias. RIPPLE is not as good as CONVIT, another model with locality bias, on classification tasks, and also does not show advantages on the detection task.

A2: Ripple attention does not put a hard constraint on locality. It only assumes the upper bound of weights of the closer vicinal groups is larger than the one of the distal groups. This soft constraint allows the model to capture long-term dependencies. It should be interesting to evaluate the model’s robustness. We leave that as future work.
The performance of ripple attention is bottlenecked by linearized attention, which itself underperforms the softmax counterpart. Nevertheless, we find it still performs comparably to ConViT, a performant baseline that directly improves on the softmax attention, showing the effectiveness of our approach.
 
> Q3: Discussion on some other baselines is missed. A bunch of works have also introduce locality bias into transformers, eg., constraining the range of attention [3], or combining convolution and self-attention [4]. Experiments with all these baselines can be time-consuming, but at least some justification of the relation between RIPPLE and the prior arts is helpful.

A3: Thanks for your insightful comments! We add a paragraph in Section 6 to highlight the differences between previous work and ours. To summarize, our method is different from previous methods in that we directly model the locality inside the attention mechanism while still preserving the ability to capture global dependencies, without the help of introducing convolutional kernels or limiting receptive fields. Furthermore, ripple attention runs in sub-quadratic complexity so that the quadratic bottleneck in vision transformers can be greatly alleviated. Withit our framework, one could potentially incorporate the relative locality into the attention mechanism while enjoying the same complexity as convolutional modules. We consider this as a solid contribution to the community.
 
> Q4: The authors may also compare to some baselines of linearized attention. It seems the authors make some changes on previous linearized attention schemes, such as using a two-layer MLP instead of random features. Some ablation study on these changes can help clarify the contribution of the locality constraint itself.

A4: We conducted an ablation study in Appendix C.1, demonstrating the difference of various linearized attention schemes.
 
> Q5: In the experiments the authors show that a hard-coded spatial weights is worse than learning the weights using stick-breaking transformation (RIPPLE vs. Fixed-RIPPLE). So if we don't have any constraint on the spatial weighting (except for positivity and unit sum), can the network still learn the local bias?

A5: We investigated the setting where no constraint on the spatial weighting (except for positivity and unit sum) is assumed. We denote this method by RIPPLE-w/o SBT and the result can be found in Table 4. Although still better than baseline, it performs much worse than our full model; this indicates it can only learn the locality bias to a limited extent.
 
> Q6: It seems the authors empirically choose the first 9 self-attention blocks to replace with RIPPLE. Does this setting apply to different tasks?

A6: For detection transformers, we apply RIPPLE to all layers since the transformer encoder is shallow, as mentioned in Section 4.1.

content.title: Summary of updates
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their insightful suggestions! We revised the paper according to all the comments and suggestions, and here is a summary of updates:
- We add a paragraph in related work (Section 6) to highlight the difference between prior work and ours.
- In Appendix D.2, we conduct further experiments to investigate different schemes of parameterizing spatial weights and find that our approach gives a good trade-off between accuracy and complexity.
- In Appendix D.3, we give a quantitative analysis on the evolution of spatial weights during training. In particular, we measure the Jensen-Shannon divergence between distributions induced by our spatial weight and exponentially decayed weights. The plot demonstrates that ripple attention learns to balance global and local information, and then tends to favor local correlations yet permit long-term dependencies.
- We correct the typo and grammar accordingly.
